title: Khawaja Asif Challenges Mohsin Naqvi to Fix Pakistan From Within Before Demanding System Overhaul
excerpt: Pakistan's Defence Minister fires back at Interior Minister's call for governance 'hard reset,' urging him to implement the National Action Plan and reform cricket first.
body:
• Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif publicly challenged Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi to implement the National Action Plan and fix the Pakistan Cricket Board before calling for a broader governance overhaul.
  • Naqvi had declared at the Pakistan Economic Summit that the country’s governance system had “collapsed” and called for new provinces or administrative units to improve public service delivery.
  • Asif argued that institutional reforms should be debated in Parliament and cabinet rather than announced at business forums, and noted Naqvi had held powerful positions for 3.5 years without initiating change.
  • The exchange has exposed deepening rifts within the Shehbaz Sharif government, with PM’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah also criticizing Naqvi’s remarks.

Naqvi Declares System ‘Collapsed’

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi set off a political firestorm when he told the Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad that the country’s governance system had “collapsed” and was no longer capable of addressing fundamental challenges. Naqvi called for a “hard reset” — proposing new provinces or administrative units to improve governance, justice, and public service delivery.

The remarks were striking coming from a sitting cabinet minister in Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government. Naqvi, who also serves as chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB), effectively argued that the existing parliamentary and administrative framework had failed.

Asif Fires Back on X

Defence Minister Khawaja Asif responded swiftly in a series of posts on X, agreeing in principle that Pakistan’s governance needed reform but rejecting the way Naqvi chose to raise the issue.

“Begin the change in the system with the implementation of NAP; begin the change in the system with your ministry. The entire nation is with you.”

— Khawaja Asif, Pakistan Defence Minister

Asif argued that constitutional changes of the magnitude Naqvi was proposing should be debated in Parliament and the federal cabinet — not announced before business audiences. He pointedly noted that Naqvi, despite holding one of the country’s most powerful portfolios, rarely attended parliamentary or cabinet sessions.

“Better late than never,” Asif said, noting that Naqvi had occupied some of Pakistan’s most influential positions for the past three-and-a-half years and could have initiated reform efforts during that time.

National Action Plan as the Test Case

Asif zeroed in on the National Action Plan (NAP), the counter-terrorism framework introduced after the devastating 2014 Army Public School attack in Peshawar. Citing recent remarks by ISPR Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, Asif noted that of the NAP’s 13 points, the single point assigned to the armed forces was being implemented “through sacrifices of lives.”

The remaining 12 points — covering terrorism financing, hate speech, criminal justice reform, and extremism — fall under the Interior Ministry’s jurisdiction and have yet to be fully implemented, Asif argued. If Naqvi wanted to prove his commitment to systemic change, the NAP was the place to start.

Cricket Catches a Stray

In a separate post, Asif took aim at Naqvi’s stewardship of the PCB. “Bring about a revolution in the PCB. There is no parliament, prime minister or outdated system stopping you there,” he wrote.

The PCB has faced sustained public criticism over administrative instability, frequent coaching changes, and poor team performance. Bangladesh clean-swept Pakistan on home soil in 2024, inflicting defeats of 104 and 78 runs in the Test series, followed by a 2-1 ODI series win. Asif’s point was clear: Naqvi had unchecked authority over cricket and had not delivered results even there.

Rifts Within the Sharif Government

The exchange has exposed fault lines within Pakistan’s ruling coalition. PM’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah joined the criticism, telling a gathering in Azad Jammu and Kashmir that those who had “achieved in three-and-a-half years what others took decades to accomplish” were now arguing the system could no longer function.

Meanwhile, the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) has referred Naqvi’s governance proposal to its top leadership for review. Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah rejected the idea outright, and Sindhi nationalist groups demanded Naqvi’s resignation. MQM-P seized the moment to reiterate its longstanding demand for Karachi to become a separate province.

What’s Next

The governance debate is unfolding against a backdrop of broader instability in Pakistan, including protests across Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Whether Naqvi’s proposals gain traction or remain rhetorical will likely depend on how the Sharif government manages these internal tensions in the months ahead.
